newsitem.title: JAPAN: WTO liquor tax ruling severe for Japan -- MOF's Kubo.
newsitem.headline: WTO liquor tax ruling severe for Japan -- MOF's Kubo.

text.p: The World Trade Organisation's (WTO) ruling that Japan's liquor taxation system runs counter to the international trade body's rules is severe for Japan, Minister of Finance Wataru Kubo told a news conference on Friday.

Kubo said Japan had not decided how to respond to the WTO ruling, but would consider how to deal with the tax issue before it makes a formal response to the WTO. Under WTO rules, Japan should respond to the WTO within 30 days of a ruling.
Finance Ministry officials have said in recent months that the ministry may need to revise liquor taxes if the WTO's ruling failed to support Japan's claims.
The EU has claimed that Japan taxes imported spirits at rates more than six times higher than those imposed on popular domestic products called shochu.

Kubo also said there were no differences between Japan and the United States over interpretation of a joint memorandum on an insurance dispute which he and U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky signed in Washington this week.
Under the memorandum, Japanese insurers will be barred from entering the so-called "third-sector" domestic insurance market until December 31, 1996.

Barshefsky said this week that Japanese insurers will not be allowed to enter the third-sector market unless a comprehensive agreement is reached. Kubo has said Japanese firms will be allowed to enter the "third-sector" insurance market if a dispute with the United States is not solved by the new December 15 deadline.

Kubo said Japan's ambassador to the United States Kunihiko Saito met Barshefsky on Thursday in Washington to clarify the remarks. "Barshefsky told Saito that she did not explain the matter satisfactorily and she said she would correct the remarks at an appropriate time," Kubo said.
"It's very regrettable if any differences exist in interpretation of the Japan-U.S. agreement."
At issue is Japan's $382 billion domestic insurance market.

The United States is pressing Japan to open its primary life and casualty markets insurance markets but it wants to prevent Japan's "third sector"-- the personal accident and health care insurance sectors -- in which foreign firms have a strong foothold, from being opened to Japanese insurers in the interim.
